topic: dipping beeswax candles: wax temperature, build rate, wick centring and bloom in storage

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: wax thermometer zaciśniety na kadzi; referent nieosadzony 'alarm panel' z innej dziedziny technicznej

base: I have begun dipping candles from beeswax and the finish comes out lumpy.
A dipping rack stands beside the vat and holds a dozen pairs at once.
A wax thermometer is clamped to the vat and shows tenths of a degree.
The new candles have ridges along their length and a thick foot at the bottom.
Is the wax too cool, or am I dipping far too fast between coats?
Ridges nearly always mean cool wax rather than any fault in your timing.
Beeswax wants about seventy degrees for dipping and it stiffens quickly below that.
The thick foot comes from wax draining down and setting before you lift clear.
Dip in one steady movement and lift at the same speed every single time.
I held the wax steadier and the ridges have almost entirely disappeared.
The candles build very slowly, though, and take thirty dips to reach any thickness.
The wax thermometer reads seventy four degrees for most of the afternoon.
Is that a little too warm for building the candle up quickly enough?
Seventy four is warm, so each coat melts back part of the previous one.
Let the vat drop to about sixty eight and the candles will grow faster.
Hang each pair for a full minute between dips so the coat sets properly.
Twenty dips at the right heat beat forty dips at the wrong one.
Cooling the vat has worked and twenty dips now give a proper candle.
The candles hanging on the dipping rack are all slightly different in thickness.
Those at the outer ends come out thinner than the pairs in the middle.
Is that the wax level dropping, or does the vat cool unevenly across it?
It is the wax level, since the outer pairs reach the wax a moment later.
Top the vat up with fresh wax after every third round of dipping.
Move the outer pairs inward halfway through, so every candle sees both positions.
Stir the vat gently before each round to even the heat right through.
Topping up and swapping positions has made the whole batch far more even.
The candles burn well, though the flame gutters and the wick leans over.
Wax runs down one side and leaves a deep channel in the candle.
Is the wick too large for the diameter, or simply badly centred?
A leaning wick nearly always means the wick sits off the centre line.
Straighten each pair by hand while the wax is still soft after dipping.
A wick that is too large burns a wide pool and floods one side.
Try a smaller braid on the next batch and compare the two burning together.
Straightening while warm cured the lean and the smaller braid burns much cleaner.
The candles now burn down evenly and leave almost nothing on the holder.
Stored in a drawer, however, they have gone dull and faintly white outside.
Is that bloom a fault, or does it simply rub off with cloth?
Bloom is normal on beeswax and many people take it as a mark of quality.
Rub it gently with a soft cloth and the shine returns at once.
Warm storage slows the bloom, though it never stops it for very long.
Leave the candles you sell unpolished and explain the bloom to your buyers.
